title: Ultrasonic Testing for Pulp & Paper Mills | UT Inspection
description: UT thickness and weld inspection for US pulp and paper mills: digesters, liquor tanks, boilers, dryer cans. Technicians mobilized to your mill. Get a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Pulp and Paper Mills in the United States
html:
Ultrasonic testing for pulp and paper mills in the United States means thickness surveys and weld examinations on digesters, liquor tanks and piping, boiler pressure parts and dryer cans, carried out while the mill is down or while a given vessel is isolated. Atlantis mobilizes ASNT SNT-TC-1A qualified Level II technicians to your mill for the agreed scope and returns thickness grids and indication reports that your engineers and boiler inspector can act on. Send the scope and we will request a UT inspection quote.

What ultrasonic testing covers in a kraft mill

A kraft mill is a chemical plant wrapped around a pressure-vessel fleet. Wood chips are cooked in a digester, spent liquor is concentrated and burned in a recovery boiler, and the chemicals come back through white liquor and green liquor systems. Each stage puts a different steel in a different environment, so a useful ultrasonic scope starts by naming the asset and the mechanism you are worried about rather than asking for a generic thickness check.

Ultrasonic thickness testing answers one question well: how much wall is left at a stated location. It is the right tool for general thinning, for pitting that has not yet broken through, and for grid surveys that show where a vessel is losing metal faster than the rest of it. Manual angle-beam examination of welds is a second use, applied where your procedure and the governing code call for volumetric examination of a butt weld. Neither use replaces surface methods for cracks that open to the surface, which is why our magnetic particle and liquid penetrant pages for the same mills sit beside this one.

Digesters: shell thickness, cladding and weld seams

Continuous digesters are tall vertical vessels built from stacked shell courses, with screens, extraction lines and a top separator where flow conditions change. Batch digesters are shorter pressure vessels that cycle through heating and cooling every cook, which adds fatigue to the list of concerns. Both sit in hot, alkaline service, and thinning tends to concentrate where flow velocity changes, at liquor extraction nozzles, around screens, and in the vapor space above the liquor level.

Some digesters carry stainless cladding or overlay in selected zones. A thickness reading on clad plate needs a technique that states what the gauge actually measured, because the instrument can report total wall, base metal, or a blend of the two depending on setup. We document the setup on the report so your engineer can compare this outage with the last one on the same basis. Where the digester is treated as a pressure vessel under ASME Section VIII and jurisdictional rules, the examination plan is written to the code of construction your inspector already works to.

Caustic stress corrosion cracking is the mechanism that makes digester inspection more than a thickness exercise. API 571 describes it as cracking of carbon steel in hot caustic, concentrated at welds and cold-worked areas that were not stress relieved. Ultrasonic thickness readings will not find those cracks. A wet fluorescent magnetic particle examination of the weld seams is the usual screening tool, and we cover it on the MT page for pulp and paper. Where a crack is found, depth sizing and the repair decision belong to your engineer, using our location and length data.

Recovery and power boilers: drums, tubes and headers

Power boilers and recovery boilers in US mills are regulated under state boiler law, which generally adopts ASME Section I for new construction and the National Board Inspection Code, NBIC, for repairs and alterations. Your jurisdictional or insurance inspector decides what is acceptable. Our part is accurate data: a numbered tube map, thickness at each location, and a clear note of anything that falls below the minimum your engineer has stated. The detailed tube method is on the ultrasonic boiler tube inspection page.

The Black Liquor Recovery Boiler Advisory Committee, BLRBAC, publishes guidance on safe operation and inspection practice that many mills follow alongside the code. The furnace is unusual because molten smelt and water must never meet, so a wall that is thinning toward a leak matters more here than in an ordinary boiler. When a reading approaches the limit your engineer gave us, the technician flags it to your representative at the time of the reading, not when the report is issued.

Lower-furnace tubes in recovery boilers are commonly composite, a carbon steel core with a stainless outer layer, and cracking in that outer layer calls for specialist techniques we do not offer on this page. We can still map remaining wall on the carbon steel side where the geometry allows, and we state clearly what the reading does and does not represent.

Liquor tanks, piping and dryer cans

Black liquor, white liquor and green liquor tanks are large carbon steel vessels, and mills often apply the thinking in API 653 when planning floor and shell surveys even where the tank is not formally under that standard. Our tank inspection page describes the broader scope. For liquor tanks specifically, the useful ultrasonic work is a shell course grid, a check of nozzle necks and reinforcing pads, and floor readings taken from the outside where access allows.

Liquor piping behaves like process piping with a hot, abrasive, scaling fluid inside. Thinning concentrates at elbows, reducers and below-grade or insulated runs. We survey the condition monitoring locations your mill has already established, so each outage adds a data point to a trend your reliability group can read. If your mill does not yet have numbered locations, our piping circuit survey sets them up. The job-level detail is on the ultrasonic pipe thickness testing page.

Paper machine dryer cans and Yankee dryers are rotating pressure vessels that many mills manage under ASME Section VIII and their state boiler program. Shell thickness around the circumference and the condition of welds at heads are standard ultrasonic checks. Because the shell is rotating equipment with a polished or machined surface, the technician uses couplant and a scanning pattern chosen to protect that surface, and the report records the angular positions used.

Technique details that matter on a mill outage

  • Scale and liquor deposits. Digester and tank walls carry hard scale. Readings on scale read high or fail to return a clean back wall, so the scope should say who removes it, to what level, and at which locations.
  • Calibration. We calibrate on blocks of the same acoustic material and bracket the expected thickness, following the practice in ASME Section V Article 5 and ASTM E797 for manual contact thickness measurement. The block and instrument serial numbers go on the report.
  • Surface temperature. Equipment returning from service can still be hot. High-temperature probes and couplants are rated for stated limits, and a surface that exceeds the limit is rescheduled, not measured through.
  • Coverage. A grid with stated spacing is more useful than scattered points. The grid origin, spacing and direction are drawn on the sketch so the next survey can repeat it.
  • Weld examination. Where a butt weld is to be examined with angle-beam technique, the procedure follows ASME Section V Article 4 and the acceptance criteria your code of construction names.

Codes and who decides acceptance

The code of construction sets the acceptance criteria, the owner or user sets the minimum acceptable thickness, and a jurisdictional, insurance or authorized inspector accepts or rejects the equipment. Atlantis reports what the instrument found against the criteria you give us. We do not calculate remaining life, set inspection intervals or judge fitness for service; your engineer does that from our data. The documents most often named on pulp and paper scopes are ASME Section I and Section VIII for pressure parts, the NBIC for repairs, ASME Section V for the examination method, API 571 for damage mechanisms, and BLRBAC guidance for recovery boilers. TAPPI publishes technical information papers on digester and tank inspection, and your mill may reference them in its own program.

When ultrasonic testing is the wrong method

Ultrasonic examination is the wrong first choice for surface cracking on ferromagnetic welds, because a magnetic particle examination finds those faster and shows them directly; see the MT page. It is also the wrong choice for tight surface-breaking flaws in stainless piping and cladding, where liquid penetrant is more direct; see the PT page. If your question is about cracking in the stainless layer of composite tubes, or about volumetric flaws that need sizing by methods beyond manual angle beam, that is outside what we offer on this page. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States; where code calls for it, your mill uses a licensed radiography contractor.

What the report contains

ItemWhat you receive
Component identificationEquipment number, location, nominal and minimum thickness as supplied by you
ProcedureWritten procedure and revision, with the code section it follows

EvaluationReading compared with the minimum you provided, reported as meets or below
ReviewASNT Level III review of the report before it is issued

What to send for a quote

  • Equipment list with tag numbers and a sketch or drawing of each vessel, tank or tube bank
  • Material, nominal thickness and minimum required thickness
  • Prior thickness data if you have it, so we can place readings at the same points
  • Code or specification governing the work, and the owner's acceptance criteria
  • Surface condition, insulation, scale removal and who provides it
  • Surface temperatures expected during the survey
  • Access method, such as scaffold, lift or rope access set by the mill
  • Site address, badging or safety orientation requirements and permit process

Planning a mill outage in the United States

Annual and semiannual outages compress every trade into a short window, so ultrasonic work is sequenced after cleaning and before coating or insulation is replaced. Confined space entry into digesters and tanks is governed by 29 CFR 1910.146 and the mill's own permit program, and our technicians follow your entry procedure, atmospheric testing and rescue plan. Lockout, hot work and scaffold permits are issued by the mill. Atlantis technicians travel to your site with their own gauges and calibration blocks, and the schedule is agreed once the scope and access dates are fixed. The same coordination logic is described on our turnarounds and shutdowns page.

Where we work in the US for pulp and paper

Pulp and paper capacity clusters in the Southeast and the Pacific Northwest, with notable activity along the Gulf Coast and in the mid-South. These city pages describe how Atlantis mobilizes to each region.

  • Mobile, Alabama: Gulf Coast mills and chemical plants on the Mobile River and bay.
  • Savannah, Georgia: coastal Georgia mills and the port that serves them.
  • Jacksonville, Florida: northeast Florida mills along the St. Johns and the coast.
  • Charleston, South Carolina: Lowcountry mills and a deepwater port.
  • Richmond, Virginia: Mid-Atlantic mills and energy plants along the James River corridor.
  • Memphis, Tennessee: mid-South converting and board mills on the Mississippi.
  • Shreveport, Louisiana: north Louisiana and East Texas mills.
  • Tacoma, Washington: Puget Sound mills and the Pacific Northwest port system.
  • Spokane, Washington: inland Northwest mills and wood-products plants.
  • Portland, Oregon: Columbia River and Willamette Valley mills.

Training your own technicians

Many mills keep a small in-house team for between-outage readings. Our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training are built on SNT-TC-1A, and the practice work is available through the ultrasonic testing simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A your company certifies its own personnel under its written practice, and we can help you build that document through written practice development. Manufacturing teams can also look at our manufacturing NDT training.

What we do not do here

We do not run radiography, we do not size cracking in composite tube cladding, and we do not decide remaining life or repair scope. Our procedure development service can write the UT procedure your inspector will review before the outage. The national page for the method is ultrasonic testing, and the code basics are explained in our guide to ASME Section V Article 5.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing find caustic cracking in a digester?
faq.a: Not reliably. Ultrasonic thickness readings measure remaining wall, and caustic stress corrosion cracks are surface-breaking flaws at welds. Wet fluorescent magnetic particle examination is the usual screening method, and ultrasonic work is added where a crack needs its depth checked by your engineer.

faq.q: Do you work inside digesters and liquor tanks?
faq.a: Technicians enter vessels only under the mill's confined space permit program and 29 CFR 1910.146. We follow your atmospheric testing, lockout and rescue arrangements, and the mill supplies scaffolding, lighting and cleaning.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a boiler or vessel thickness survey?
faq.a: Send tag numbers, drawings or tube maps, material and nominal and minimum thickness, prior readings, the governing code, surface condition, access method and site badging steps. That is enough to scope grids and technician days.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the readings?
faq.a: Your engineer sets the minimum thickness, and your jurisdictional, insurance or authorized inspector accepts the equipment. Atlantis reports each reading against the minimum you supply and flags anything below it, but acceptance stays with the owner and inspector.

faq.q: Can you measure through paint or insulation?
faq.a: Through intact coating is possible when the gauge technique is verified on that coating and the report says what was measured. Insulation has to be removed at the test location. Where neither is practical, the survey is scoped with windows cut by the mill.

faq.q: Do you inspect recovery boiler floor tubes?
faq.a: We can map remaining wall on the carbon steel side where geometry allows. Cracking in the stainless layer of composite tubes needs specialist techniques that we do not offer, so we state the limit of the reading in the report.

faq.q: Is this the same as an API 510 or boiler inspection?
faq.a: No. The authorized or jurisdictional inspector is the inspector of record. Atlantis supplies the ultrasonic data and written report that inspector reviews, and does not calculate remaining life or set intervals.

faq.q: How do you handle hot equipment after shutdown?
faq.a: Readings are taken only within the temperature rating of the probe and couplant, which the procedure states. If a surface is too hot, the technician waits for it to cool or moves to another area, and the report records any location not measured.

faq.q: Can you work to a TAPPI guideline or our own mill standard?
faq.a: Yes. Send the document and we will follow its location map and recording format, while keeping the method itself to ASME Section V practice. TAPPI papers are guidance, so we confirm with your engineer which parts apply.
